title: Ironing out the details: Fe homeostasis in the shoot and root is regulated by distinct actions of BTS/BTSL1/2 and bHLH IVc subgroup transcription factors
content: You may have had your iron (Fe) levels checked during a medical checkup, but a plant needs to keep track of its own Fe levels. For plants, Fe serves as a enzymatic cofactor for hormone synthesis and as an essential building block of enzymes involved in photosynthetic chains and in redox reactions, among other roles (Rout and Sahoo 2015). Plants need to keep a fine Fe balance, as too much or too little affects development, in part due to the ability of Fe to catalyze the formation of free radicals that damage the cell. There are 2 well-described mechanisms of Fe uptake from soil by the root. One is a reduction-based strategy, via reduction of ferric Fe (Fe3+) by ferric reduction oxidase 2 (FRO2) and coumarins, which create ferrous Fe (Fe2+) that is transported into the root by IRON-REGULATED TRANSPORTER 1 (IRT1) (Rout and Sahoo 2015). The second mechanism is chelation based, releasing Fe-chelating phytosiderophores into the soil and thus improving Fe mobilization back into the root by YELLOW STRIPE1 (YS1) and the related YS1-like (YSL) (Rout and Sahoo 2015).
